messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Unemployed
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory/Mechanical: Motorcycle noise, Auditory (Language): Shouting in Arabic, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Anniversaries: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event, Avoid Night: Going out at night or being outside after dark, Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
  Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Others-Would-Cope: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At nineteen, Emily had been married less than a year when she was assaulted, and she still describes her life as divided into before and after. The assault happened at night as she was walking back from a convenience store near her apartment. She remembers hearing a motorcycle idling nearby before it came closer, and then men’s voices, one of them suddenly raised in Arabic. The sharp smell of alcohol hit her before she fully understood what was happening. What stayed with her most was the combination of those sensations—the engine noise, the shouting, the stale liquor on someone’s breath—so that the event now lives in her as much through sound and smell as through images.

In the weeks afterward, those cues began to pull the memory back with shocking speed. A motorcycle passing her street could bring back the whole scene without warning, and if she heard men shouting in Arabic from a passing car or from a phone video somewhere in public, she would freeze and feel the assault rush back in full force. When the memory came, she did not just think about what happened; she heard the voices in her head as if they were happening again and sometimes caught the smell of alcohol so vividly that she would look around to see where it was coming from. Over time, the memories themselves seemed to make the world more densely packed with danger cues. She had become so sensitized to engine noise, raised male voices, and the smell of liquor that she noticed them everywhere, and ordinary surroundings began to feel littered with traps.

Emily came to believe that what happened had destroyed her basic assumptions about how the world worked. Before the assault, she said, she had assumed that if she was careful and did the right things, she would be safe; now she was certain that safety could vanish instantly and for no reason. She also judged herself harshly. She was convinced that somebody else would have stopped the event from happening, that another woman would have fought back, run faster, or somehow known what to do. Hearing a motorcycle rev or catching alcohol on a stranger’s breath did not just trigger fear; it also brought a flood of self-condemning thoughts about being weak and no longer capable, as if those sensations proved again that she had been changed into someone less competent than she used to be.

Those beliefs fed directly into the way she now watches for danger. She listens at home for any sound that might mean someone is entering, especially at night, and she checks behind her repeatedly when she does go out, certain that if she misses one sign she will be caught off guard again. What frightened her most was not only the possibility of another assault but the conviction that she would fail again if something happened. When she had a flashback, that sense of present danger intensified; her body reacted as if the assault were happening again, and she would scan doors, windows, and hallways with desperate concentration. The more she monitored for threat, the more easily fragments of the assault broke through—voices, the engine, the smell—and each recurrence seemed to confirm for her that the world was unsafe and that she was no longer able to manage it.

Her avoidance developed gradually but has become the structure of her days. She refuses to go out after dark, because nighttime feels inseparable from what happened and because every motorcycle or distant shout seems amplified once the sun goes down. She avoids dates connected to the assault, becoming tense and withdrawn as they approach, staying home and trying not to think about the calendar. She also avoids looking at or paying attention to her own body; even catching her reflection while dressing can stir up the memory too abruptly. At first these strategies felt like the only way to prevent being overwhelmed, but they have narrowed her life. Because she is unemployed, much of her time is spent inside the apartment, where she tries to control what she hears and smells, yet that has made her more reactive when she does encounter those cues. The more thoroughly she organizes life around avoiding night, anniversaries, and her own body, the less chance she has to learn that a motorcycle passing by or alcohol on someone in a grocery line is not the assault happening again. Instead, each avoidance seems to preserve the rawness of the memory and strengthen her belief that she cannot cope.

Her husband has become used to finding her checking the locks repeatedly or pausing mid-conversation because she has heard a sound outside. She knows how young she is to feel this defeated, and that thought shames her further. By the time she sought help, she was spending most evenings braced for danger, scanning for noises, and dreading sudden sensory jolts that could pull her back into the assault. She came in because she feels her world shrinking and because she is terrified that this is permanent—that she will always live as if the next motorcycle, the next shouted phrase, or the next trace of alcohol means she is back there again.
